summary: At Sand Creek US troops killed nine members of the Cheyenne Council of 44 plus several warrior society leaders; Arapaho diplomat Left Hand (Niwot) died of wounds. Council member Lean Bear had been killed earlier in 1864 under orders to kill Cheyennes wherever found. The source argues this destroyed leadership needed for later treaty-making.
verbatim_quote: U.S. troops assassinated nine members of the Cheyenne Council of 44
federal_account_contrast: Federal treaty record treats later Cheyenne signers as full tribal representatives; source shows the legitimate governing council had been decimated just before Little Arkansas 1865.
map_implication: Attach Sand Creek massacre node to the 1865 Little Arkansas and 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty nodes as 'leadership killed before signing' context.
notes: Names: White Antelope, Lone Bear, Yellow Wolf, Big Man, Bear Man, War Bonnet, Spotted Crow, Bear Robe, Little Robe (source lists a Little Robe among the dead, yet a Little Robe signs in 1865; likely two persons or an error, verify).

place: Colorado north of the South Platte; Front Range
summary: Source states land north of the South Platte had never been ceded, despite Governor Evans's claims, and that Homestead and Preemption Acts did not apply to unceded Indian land yet were used to settle it. Quotes Colorado Encyclopedia that nearly all private land in Colorado was unlawfully taken.
verbatim_quote: land north of the South Platte River had never been ceded
federal_account_contrast: Royce schedule colors Colorado plains as ceded; source asserts the area north of South Platte had no cession at the time homesteading began.
map_implication: Flag homestead-era patents north of the South Platte as issued on land not yet ceded; show date gap between settlement and any cession instrument.
notes: Which later instrument (if any) the source thinks extinguished title north of the South Platte is not stated in this chunk; cross-check with Fort Wise / ICC Docket 329 findings.

place: Platte, Republican and Smoky Hill valleys
summary: Pacific Railway Act directed the US to extinguish Indian title along the route as rapidly as possible; Interior Secretary Usher said it required removing Indians from the Platte and Republican valleys.
verbatim_quote: The United States shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act
federal_account_contrast: Railroad grants are usually shown as federal actions separate from treaties; source frames them as the driver of the 1865-1869 treaty and military campaign.
map_implication: Overlay railroad land grants (UP, Kansas Pacific, Denver Pacific) on 1851 Fort Laramie Cheyenne-Arapaho territory with grant dates preceding cessions.
notes: Cite not given by source; standard cite added by reader, verify.

summary: While Agent Leavenworth sought peace, Secretary of War Stanton said he had no treaty authority and Col. Ford was ordered to pursue active hostilities and ignore peace proposals. In Aug 1865 Gen. Dodge ordered columns to kill every male Indian over 12.
verbatim_quote: to pay no attention to any peace movements or propositions
sources_cited_by_source: Powell 1981, 394 (endnote 6); House Exec. Docs 39th Cong. 1st Sess. 575 (endnote 7)
federal_account_contrast: Adds the simultaneous war orders to the context of the Little Arkansas negotiations.
map_implication: Note on Little Arkansas 1865 node: negotiated amid standing orders for hostilities.
notes: Dodge 'kill every male over 12' order is asserted without its own endnote.

place: Mouth of the Little Arkansas River (Wichita, KS area)
summary: Southern chiefs signed an August 1865 truce stating they had been forced to fight Chivington's troops at Sand Creek in self-protection and had escaped an intended massacre.
verbatim_quote: having been forced, in self-protection, to fight the United States troops under the command of Colonel J.M. Chivington, at Sand creek
federal_account_contrast: Primary text in which the tribes characterize Sand Creek as an intended massacre.
map_implication: Link quote to Sand Creek massacre point.

place: Mouth of the Little Arkansas River, Kansas
instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Oct 14 1865 (Cheyenne-Arapaho)
instrument_cite: 14 Stat. 703; Kappler II 887 (not given by source; verify)
summary: Black Kettle and Little Raven said too few of their people were present to make a treaty; signers believed they signed only for their own bands, and commissioners Sanborn and Leavenworth told them so, which the source calls a lie. Powell says only eight lodges of more than 280 Southern lodges followed the four signing chiefs.
verbatim_quote: Only eight lodges followed them, eight lodges out of more than two hundred eighty lodges of the Southern People alone.
sources_cited_by_source: Powell 1981, 403 (endnote 11); US Archives 1865 Treaty of the Little Arkansas (endnote 9)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the treaty as tribe-wide; source says it was signed by a small minority under explicit promise it bound only their bands.
map_implication: Flag Little Arkansas 1865 cession as signed by a minority (approx. 8 of 280+ lodges) and represented as band-only.
notes: Lodge count is Powell's; secondary.

instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas 1865, post-signing addendum
summary: Three days after signing, a provision was added declaring the Cheyenne, Arapaho and Kiowa-Apache 'confederated tribes'; source says the tribes certainly did not agree.
verbatim_quote: Three days after the signing an amendment was added declaring the Cheyenne, Arapaho, and Kiowa-Apaches to be “confederated tribes” under the treaty. The tribes certainly did not agree to this.
federal_account_contrast: Text altered after execution without tribal consent per source.
map_implication: Mark Little Arkansas treaty text as containing a post-signing addition.
notes: Not a Senate amendment; added by commissioners. Categorized as illegitimate signing process.

instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas 1865, survivor reparations and 'mixed blood' grants
instrument_cite: 14 Stat. 703 (not given by source); article numbers not given by source
summary: The commission acknowledged Sand Creek and offered reparations as specified acreages to survivors, and promised 'mixed bloods' land on the never-developed Fort Wise reservation. The source states the reparations were never paid to the individuals named in the treaty.
verbatim_quote: The promised reparations for Sand Creek were never paid to the individuals named in the treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: No specific endnote for this sentence; Berthrong 1963 cited nearby
federal_account_contrast: The treaty is the first written US acknowledgment of Sand Creek atrocities; the land reparations were never delivered.
map_implication: Add 'promised, never delivered' layer for Little Arkansas survivor and mixed-blood land grants; link to Sand Creek.
notes: Source does not cite Art. 5/Art. 6 by number. Reader's understanding (verify against Kappler II 887-891): Art. 5 grants 640 acres to named persons of mixed descent; Art. 6 grants 320 acres to each named survivor who lost a husband or parents and 160 acres to each child. Source does not give acreages or names.

summary: Source notes the treaty set a precedent: the US acknowledged the atrocities of Sand Creek in writing, though the treaty lasted only two years and was never implemented.
verbatim_quote: The U.S. government acknowledged in writing the atrocities of Sand Creek.
federal_account_contrast: Federal acknowledgment of wrongdoing embedded in a treaty.
map_implication: Display Little Arkansas treaty as 'acknowledged Sand Creek; never implemented'.

place: Between the Arkansas and Platte; Smoky Hill-Republican
summary: The treaty said the new reservation south of the Arkansas would not be occupied until clear title was secured, and the tribes could keep hunting in unoccupied parts of their Arkansas-Platte country. The reservation was never established; source says the Southerners nonetheless lost the Arkansas-Platte lands.
verbatim_quote: the Southerners lost all the rich lands between the Arkansas and the Platte Rivers
federal_account_contrast: Royce may show this as a clean 1865 cession; source stresses the retained hunting right and a reservation never created.
map_implication: Show 1865 Little Arkansas reservation as promised but never established; mark Arkansas-Platte hunting rights as reserved.
notes: Source does not give reservation boundaries; the treaty text should be consulted.

instrument: Little Arkansas Treaty, later adhesions (Wynkoop councils 1866)
summary: Maj. Wynkoop got Medicine Arrows, Big Head and Dog Soldier leaders to sign the Little Arkansas treaty by bribing with supplies and threatening attack. Agent Leavenworth complained Wynkoop's reports hid the Cheyenne determination to keep the Smoky Hill country at any cost.
verbatim_quote: Wynkoop badgered and threatened these leaders until they signed, bribing them with supplies and threatening them with military attacks.
federal_account_contrast: Adhesions appear in the federal record as consent to cede Smoky Hill; a contemporaneous agent disputed that.
map_implication: Flag Smoky Hill portion of the 1865 cession as contested: adhesions obtained by threat and supplies.

instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas 1865, Senate amendment
summary: Under pressure from Kansans, the Senate amended the treaty so the reservation could include no land in Kansas. Black Kettle and Little Robe signed the amended treaty in Nov 1866, but the Dog Soldiers and many Southern Cheyennes did not recognize it; Black Kettle had already repudiated the Smoky Hill cession.
verbatim_quote: the Senate mandated that the Cheyenne and Arapaho reservation would not include any territory within the boundaries of Kansas
federal_account_contrast: Amendment accepted only by two chiefs; much of the tribe never assented.
map_implication: Mark Little Arkansas as Senate-amended with partial (two-chief) assent only.
notes: Technically assent was obtained from some chiefs, so not wholly 'no consent'.

place: Fort Larned, KS; Pawnee Fork; Smoky Hill Road
summary: Gen. Hancock marched 1,400 troops with Custer's 7th Cavalry into Cheyenne country, burned a large Cheyenne-Sioux village on April 19 1867 and more villages after. Sherman wrote it made little difference whether Indians were coaxed out by commissioners or killed.
verbatim_quote: it makes little difference whether they be coaxed out by Indian Commissioners or killed
federal_account_contrast: Medicine Lodge 1867 followed directly on this campaign; military duress context absent from treaty record.
map_implication: Annotate Medicine Lodge 1867 as negotiated after 1867 village burnings; the 1867 Peace Commission act authorized 4,000 volunteers if peace failed.

instrument: Act of July 20 1867 creating Indian Peace Commission
summary: The act creating the Peace Commission provided that if commissioners could not achieve peace, 4,000 volunteers would be raised to force the 'hostile Indians' onto reservations.
verbatim_quote: they should raise 4,000 volunteers to force the “hostile Indians” onto reservations
federal_account_contrast: Statutory threat of force built into the treaty mandate.
map_implication: Note statutory force clause on Medicine Lodge treaty node.
notes: Cite not given by source; standard cite added by reader, verify.

place: Medicine Lodge Creek, KS, about 60 mi south of Fort Larned
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 593; Kappler II 984 (not given by source; verify)
summary: Fourteen Cheyenne and eight Arapaho chiefs signed; the bands of Roman Nose and Medicine Arrows stayed away. Arapahos were described as destitute; gifts of food, ammunition and cloth likely motivated signing. Tribes later said they had not understood the reservation location.
verbatim_quote: These desperately needed provisions likely motivated the harassed tribes, trying to survive as the bison decreased, to agree to the treaty.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats Medicine Lodge as a full tribal cession; source notes absent bands, destitution and misunderstanding of boundaries.
map_implication: Flag Medicine Lodge 1867 cession: signed amid destitution, key bands absent, boundaries not understood.

place: Western Indian Territory south of Kansas line; south of Arkansas River
summary: The treaty created a reservation just south of the Kansas border, reserved hunting on any lands south of the Arkansas while buffalo ranged, barred white settlement on the old 1865 reservation for three years, and promised agent, physician, schools, implements and 30 years of annuities. Source says it was never adhered to in its original terms; no reservation was established in 1868.
verbatim_quote: reserve the right to hunt on any lands south of the Arkansas so long as the buffalo may range thereon in such numbers as to justify the chase
federal_account_contrast: Adds reserved hunting right and three-year settlement bar to the cession framing.
map_implication: Draw Medicine Lodge 1867 Cheyenne-Arapaho reservation (Cherokee Outlet area) as promised land never occupied; add hunting-rights zone south of the Arkansas.
notes: Boundaries not given in source; take from treaty Art. 2.

summary: Source quotes NPS that the Interior Secretary in 1873 said civilizing the Indian was impossible while buffalo remained, and that the Army provided free ammunition to hide hunters. About 7.5 million bison killed 1872-74.
verbatim_quote: the Army provided free ammunition to hide hunters, who brought bison to the brink of extinction
sources_cited_by_source: NPS, What Happened to the Bison? (endnote 20); Berthrong 1963, 381 (endnote 26)
federal_account_contrast: Bison destruction undercut the Medicine Lodge hunting right.
map_implication: Link Medicine Lodge hunting right to bison extermination as practical nullification.
notes: Army ammunition claim is NPS-sourced; widely repeated but contested in detail.

summary: Former Commissioner Manypenny suggested in 1880 that Sheridan and Hazen diverted Medicine Lodge Treaty supply money to the winter campaign. Source says the US used hunger as a weapon.
verbatim_quote: Sheridan and Hazen diverted money from the Medicine Lodge Treaty supplies to the winter campaign
federal_account_contrast: Annuity diversion not in treaty record.
map_implication: Note possible diversion of Medicine Lodge annuity funds 1868.
notes: 'Suggested' per source; single source.

place: Washita River, Indian Territory (near Cheyenne, OK; approx 35.62N, -99.69W)
summary: A week after Hazen refused Black Kettle's peace request at Fort Cobb and told him not to come there, Custer attacked Black Kettle's village on the Washita, killing Black Kettle, 9-20 warriors and 18-40 women and children. Sherman distinguished it from Sand Creek because Fort Cobb had refused protection.
verbatim_quote: He declined to offer to make peace and warned the chief not to come to Fort Cobb
federal_account_contrast: Occurred within the Medicine Lodge treaty period against a signatory chief seeking peace.
map_implication: Add Washita massacre point; link to Medicine Lodge 1867 as breach context.
notes: Lat/long from reader's knowledge of Washita Battlefield NHS; verify.

place: Fort Cobb; Fort Sill; Staked Plains
summary: Little Robe, Yellow Bear and 19 leaders surrendered at Fort Cobb with their people starving. Custer took Cheyenne chiefs Big Head, Dull Knife (Lean Face) and Fat Bear hostage under threat of hanging; Big Head and Dull Knife were later killed at Fort Hays 'attempting to escape'.
verbatim_quote: Custer took Cheyenne chiefs Big Head, Dull Knife (Lean Face), and Fat Bear hostage, using the threat of hanging them
federal_account_contrast: Concentration onto the reservation was by starvation and hostage-taking.
map_implication: Tag 1869 settlement onto reservation as coerced (hostages, starvation).
notes: This Dull Knife (Lean Face) is a Southern Cheyenne, not the Northern chief Morning Star; verify.

summary: Maj. Carr's troops defeated the Dog Soldiers at Summit Springs, killing 52 including Tall Bull. Berthrong: this ended Cheyenne occupation of the region between the Platte and Arkansas.
verbatim_quote: The Battle of Summit Springs thus ended Cheyenne occupation and use of the region between the Platte and Arkansas rivers.
federal_account_contrast: Military defeat, not a treaty, ended occupation of NE Colorado.
map_implication: Add Summit Springs point in Colorado; note that effective dispossession of the Platte-Arkansas country was military.
notes: Source calls it a battle; listed as MASSACRE category for mass violence; adjust if needed. Exact date not given in source (May-Aug 1869 campaign).

place: North Fork of the Canadian River, Indian Territory
instrument_cite: EO date not given by source (reader: Aug 10 1869; verify)
summary: The tribes rejected the Medicine Lodge reservation (salty Salt Fork water, near Kansas settlers) and Grant created a roughly 4.3 million acre reservation on the North Fork of the Canadian by executive order. Source calls this evidence treaties were arbitrary to the US.
verbatim_quote: By executive order, President Grant created a new Cheyenne and Arapaho reservation on the north fork of the Canadian River
federal_account_contrast: The reservation actually lived on was never secured by treaty; the treaty reservation was never ceded until 1872/1890.
map_implication: Draw 1869 EO reservation (4,294,412 acres per Berthrong) distinct from 1867 treaty reservation.

nations: Southern Cheyenne;Southern Arapaho;Wichita and Affiliated Bands
summary: More than 760,000 acres of the Cheyenne-Arapaho EO reservation were taken in 1872 and assigned to the Wichitas and Affiliated Bands.
verbatim_quote: In 1872 more than 760,000 acres of the Cheyenne-Arapaho Executive Order Reservation were taken away and assigned to the Wichitas and Affiliated Bands.
federal_account_contrast: No consent instrument named.
map_implication: Show 1872 Wichita carve-out from C&A EO reservation.

instrument: 1872 Arapaho agreement relinquishing Medicine Lodge reservation
summary: A Southern Arapaho delegation in Washington, under pressure, signed an agreement relinquishing title to the Medicine Lodge reservation; no Cheyennes attended. Source says the Medicine Lodge reservation had never been formally ceded.
verbatim_quote: No Cheyennes attended these meetings.
federal_account_contrast: A joint reservation relinquished by one of two nations.
map_implication: Flag 1872 relinquishment of Medicine Lodge reservation as Arapaho-only, Cheyenne excluded.
notes: Source later (p.225) says the tribes never ceded the Outlet land until 1890; reconcile (1872 agreement likely unratified).

summary: Cattlemen paid key tribal members, agency staff and traders to secure signatures granting grazing on about 2.4 million acres at two cents per acre; tribes were restricted to 426,202 of 4,294,412 acres. Agent Miles held monopolies and later skimmed surplus-land payments. Cleveland expelled the cattlemen in 1885.
verbatim_quote: the Cheyennes and Arapahoes [being] restricted to a mere 426,202 acres of their 4,294,412-acre reservation
federal_account_contrast: Leasing is invisible in cession maps.
map_implication: Optional layer: 1883-85 grazing leases covering ~2.4 million acres.

instrument: Attorney contract (10% fee) with tribal chiefs
summary: Former agent Miles and frontier attorneys supposedly representing the tribes held a vague contract, signed deceptively with a tiny group of chiefs, for 10 percent of any settlement; they held secret communications with the commissioners. $67,000 of tribal money went to the attorneys.
verbatim_quote: It was often difficult to determine whose side the attorneys were on.
federal_account_contrast: Tribal counsel had a financial stake in the cession.
map_implication: Annotate 1890 agreement: tribal attorneys conflicted, $67,000 fee.
notes: Source prints 'May 1869 in Oklahoma City'; almost certainly a typo for 1889 (Oklahoma City founded 1889).

instrument: Jerome (Cherokee) Commission agreement with Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1890
instrument_cite: Ratified Act of March 3 1891 (source gives date only; reader: 26 Stat. 1022, verify)
summary: Jerome threatened that the Dawes Act would be forced on them, that Medicine Lodge annuities would lapse, and that the Indian 'will starve'. Beef rations had been cut in half the prior year. Hagan judges it highly likely that attorney money bought the signatures of a handful who recruited others.
verbatim_quote: If you don’t do what the President wants you to do, the law of Congress will be put in force
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows a ratified agreement; source documents coercion and probable bribery.
map_implication: Flag 1890-91 Cheyenne-Arapaho cession as obtained by threats, ration cuts and probable bribery.

instrument: Jerome Commission agreement 1890; Medicine Lodge Treaty three-fourths clause (Art. 12)
summary: Secretary Noble told Jerome to get three-fourths of adult males as Medicine Lodge required, 'but close with a majority if you cannot get more'. Agent Ashley claimed only 618 adult males so 464 signatures sufficed; Berthrong finds this not credible and thinks 680 were needed but not available. Most Cheyennes boycotted; a January 1891 protest by seven Cheyenne chiefs was ignored.
verbatim_quote: but close with a majority if you cannot get more
federal_account_contrast: Treaty-required consent threshold likely not met; signature count manipulated.
map_implication: Mark 1891 cession as likely failing Medicine Lodge three-fourths requirement (Lone Wolf-type issue).
notes: Article number not given by source (Art. 12 is reader's knowledge). Protesters: Old Crow, Young Whirlwind, Little Big Jake, White Horse, White Shield, Red Moon, Wolf Face.

summary: Major parts of the Cherokee Outlet were promised to the Cheyenne and Arapaho at Medicine Lodge though already designated for the Cherokees. Noble told Jerome not to 'pay twice' for the Outlet; Jerome had the tribes sell 'any rights they might have' in either reservation, causing confusion about what was sold.
verbatim_quote: Jerome stated that the tribes were selling “any rights they might have” in either.
federal_account_contrast: Overlapping US promises to two nations.
map_implication: Show Medicine Lodge reservation overlapping Cherokee Outlet; note double promise.

summary: Price held at 50 cents per acre (about $55 per person). Allotting agents chose allotments for families who refused. Of 4,294,415 acres the tribes retained 529,692 (12 percent); 231,828 school land, 32,343 military, about 3.5 million opened in the April 19 1892 land run of 25,000-30,000 settlers.
verbatim_quote: Of the 4,294,415 acres of the reservation the Cheyennes and Arapahoes retained 529,692 acres
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows a cession; source shows forced allotment at a fraction of statutory $1.25/acre.
map_implication: Attach acreage breakdown to 1891 cession; color retained allotments separately.
notes: Category should arguably be BRIBERY_FRAUD_FORGERY or TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT; ICC_OUTCOME used loosely. Note source later says $1.5M for 4,608,878 acres (p.230), inconsistent with 4.29M acre total.

summary: Source says Boulder Chautauqua sits on land used by Left Hand's Arapahos as winter residence, 'stolen property' never compensated; Boulder was platted in 1858 and incorporated 1871 on unceded Arapaho and Cheyenne land.
verbatim_quote: the stately old buildings sit on stolen property, for which the Arapaho never received compensation
federal_account_contrast: Local land titles derive from settlement before any cession.
map_implication: Add Boulder/Chautauqua as site settled on unceded land in defiance of the 1851 treaty.
notes: Source says 'In 1851 fifty-three Anglo-American squatters platted lots' at Boulder; this is surely 1858/1859 (Boulder City Town Co. 1859). Flag as error. Also 'never compensated' conflicts with ICC award; source means no compensation specific to the site.

instrument: Fort Laramie Treaty Sept 17 1851; ICC Dockets 329, 348
instrument_cite: ICC Dockets 329, 348, 329-A, 329-B; 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 612 (cited in recs endnote 11)
summary: ICC found in 1955 the tribes owned 51,210,000 acres under the 1851 treaty, valued it at $23,500,000 as of October 14 1865 (about 45 cents/acre, method undocumented); Southern share 50.61 percent. Consideration from Fort Wise, Little Arkansas and Medicine Lodge set at $1,434,131.38.
verbatim_quote: The Commission’s records do not document how a value of only 45 cents per acre was arrived at.
sources_cited_by_source: Williams, TREC Northern Cheyenne report; ICC records
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing: claim paid; source: valuation at 1865 date, undocumented, offsets for treaty consideration.
map_implication: On 1851 Fort Laramie C-A territory, show ICC valuation ($23.5M, 45c/acre, valued as of Oct 14 1865) and note taking date set at Little Arkansas treaty.
notes: Valuation date equals Little Arkansas treaty date, implying ICC treated the 1865 treaty as the taking.

summary: Government offered $15,000,000 to settle all Southern claims, including the claim that $1,500,000 paid for the 1891 taking of 4,608,878 acres was unconscionable. Accepted 338 to 2 at Watonga after notice to 1,542 members. Source argues it was below even the inflation-adjusted 1865 half share ($22.7M) and excluded loss of life and property.
verbatim_quote: The Indian Claims Commission only considered land claims.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account: final settlement; source: inadequate, low turnout vote, no compensation for life or suffering.
map_implication: Mark C-A lands as 'extinguished by ICC payment, 1965 compromise $15M' rather than 'ceded'.
notes: Turnout ~22 percent of notified members.

summary: Tribe's TREC recommendations say the ICC valuations were biased, issues of the 1851 treaty and the illegal taking within Fort Wise 1861 boundaries were unresolved, and the tribes' petition to reserve appeal rights was barred by ICC rules, while the government could appeal. They seek to reopen the settlement.
verbatim_quote: when the Tribes inserted a petition to reserve the rights for appeal, they were automatically barred
federal_account_contrast: Tribe disputes finality of the ICC settlement.
map_implication: Note on ICC layer: tribe contests settlement finality and seeks appeal.
notes: Tribal position paper; legal characterization not independently verified.

place: Denver and ~20 Colorado towns founded before 1861
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18 1861, Senate removal of Art. 11
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 1163; Kappler II 807 (not given by source; verify)
summary: Tribe says the Senate's removal of Article 11 of Fort Wise and the amendment needed to ratify are suspicious: the amended document has erasures, possible date changes and misrepresented signatures. They say this bears directly on Denver and about 20 cities founded before 1861.
verbatim_quote: several places in the amended document contain erasures, possible date changes, and outright misrepresentation of signatures
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats Fort Wise as ratified with amendment assented to; tribe alleges forgery.
map_implication: Flag Fort Wise 1861 cession (Royce area to be determined) as contested: alleged altered amendment and signatures.
notes: Source does not say what Art. 11 provided. Reader's understanding: the original Art. 11 concerned recognition of land grants/claims to individuals (possibly town sites); verify against Kappler. Fort Wise itself is covered in other PSL chunks.

instrument_cite: 11 Stat. 749; Kappler II 594 (not given by source; verify)
summary: Tribe's recommendations refer to 'the unratified Treaty of 1851', while the narrative and ICC treat it as the basis of title to 51,210,000 acres.
verbatim_quote: The issues of the unratified Treaty of 1851
federal_account_contrast: Kappler prints 1851 Fort Laramie as a treaty; its Senate amendment (annuity term cut 50 to 10 years) and ratification status are long disputed.
map_implication: Mark 1851 Fort Laramie as 'Senate-amended; ratification status disputed'.
notes: Reader context, not from this chunk: Senate amended annuity term; some tribes' assent was gathered later. Verify.

place: Front Range to Continental Divide; Colorado
summary: Tribe says the Front Range up to the Continental Divide was legally titled to them, 100,000 trespassers mined gold in 1859, and they were never compensated for minerals or water. Also claims railroad grants, state school land (4 million acres) and CSU land (19,000 acres still held) came from their land.
verbatim_quote: The Front Range and up to the continental divide were all legally titled to the Cheyenne and Arapaho
federal_account_contrast: ICC valued only surface land; minerals extracted before cession not compensated.
map_implication: Add layer for gold-rush mining on 1851 treaty land before 1861 cession; mark CSU and state school lands derived from C-A treaty land.
notes: Tribal recommendations; figures not independently sourced.
